newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS - Mexico corn syrup battle comes to boil.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mexico corn syrup battle comes to boil.

text.p: Mexico sugar industrialists won a first tentative round in their battle to have tariffs slapped on U.S. imports of high fructose corn syrup (HFCS) as the government moved Wednesday to investigate dumping charges.

Mexican mill owners have long pushed the government to act to protect traditional sugar markets against the threat of being brushed aside by the corn-based sweetener, which is widely used in the soft drinks and food industries.
Mexico ratified Wednesday in the government's Official Gazette that it is starting an investigation against 17 firms for disloyal trade practices and dumping at prices below cost.
Most of the biggest names in the world sugar and sweetener industry are embroiled in the dumping investigation.

They include U.S. grains giant Cargill Inc., British-based sugar conglomerate Tate & Lyle Plc, specialist corn syrup producer CPC International Inc. and Archer Daniels Midland Corp. (ADM), the largest U.S. agricultural processing firm.

Evidence has been found, Mexico's Trade Ministry said, that imports of fructose enter the Mexican market, allegedly under conditions of price discrimination, and threatened to cause damage to the national sugar industry.
Named exporters and importers have 30 working days to respond and present arguments and proof so that the ministry has the necessary material to arrive at a preliminary ruling.
The Mexican Sugar Chamber, which is the umbrella group for the owners of the country's 61 active cane crushing mills, is pressing the dumping charges.
Chamber spokesmen said they believe corn syrup has been dumped on the Mexican market at loss making prices to win market share.

Carlos Artolozaga, a councellor for the chamber and a owner of two large mills, told Reuters recently the dumping charges involve around 300,000 tonnes of mainly class 55 (55 percent fructose) HFCS that came in from the United States but were not necessarily produced there.
Class 55 HFCS are not currently made in Mexico. Other types are beginning to come on line in fledging plants linked with top name backers.

Arancia Corn Products, a joint venture between Arancia and CPC International, brought a 18,000 tonnes per month plant on line late last year in Queretaro state, with plans to boost that to 60,000 tonnes per month.
Almidones Mexicanos (Almex) has a corn syrup production venture with Tate & Lyle in the western city of Guadalajara. Cargill has its own plant in Tula, Hidalgo.

The threat from high fructose is very real to the Mexican sugar industry and a source of major concern. Experts believe corn syrup demand last year was at least 450 million pounds (205,000 tonnes), may be up to 600 million pounds (270,000 tonnes).
Steve Vuilleumier, vice-president of the information services firm McKeany-Flavell Co, said recently he expected Mexico to be using two billion pounds by 2000, just short of one million tonnes.

Not only is the chamber worried about the threat of corn syrup winning over traditional markets, it is also concerned that cheap imports are keeping a lid on sugar prices, and causing industrialists financial difficulties.
